reference_audit_spec.name: HMDA-GA Fair-Lending Remediation Audit v3.0
reference_audit_spec.why_this_spec: Georgia mortgage decisions must satisfy ECOA/FHA disparate-impact doctrine. A multi-metric audit plus qualitative diagnosis provides a remediation-ready hand-off for model, compliance, and business teams.
supporting_research: Mehrabi et al. 2019 – complementary metrics catch different harms [4]
Feldman et al. 2014 – certify/remove disparate impact with legal-style thresholds [5]
Kamiran & Calders 2011 – pre-processing to repair biased training labels [6]
Bartlett et al. 2019 – historical underwriting discrimination embedded in HMDA data [3]
Duarte et al. 2012 – gender-linked informational gaps in lending [1]
Pope & Sydnor 2011 – age proxies and indirect bias in credit markets [2]

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Black applicants (34 % of the sample) are approved 64.4 % of the time vs 74.3 % for White applicants (DI = 0.896 < 0.95). Equal-opportunity and error-rate gaps are small, so the harm manifests as lower access to credit rather than higher mis-classification risk. Very small groups (≤30 rows) have unstable metrics but do not drive the disparity.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Causal chain: (a) Historical label bias – past redlining and disparate underwriting are recorded as the ‘ground truth’ approvals (Bartlett et al., 2019); (b) Representation bias – Whites out-number Blacks 1.7×, so loss minimisation weighs White errors more heavily (Mehrabi et al., 2019); (c) Proxy leakage – geographic and wealth variables correlate with race and act as stand-in predictors (Feldman et al., 2014). Because the TPR/FPR parity is high, the disparity is driven mainly by biased labels and features, not model thresholds.
qualitative.how_to_fix:
Immediate (≤2 wks):
• Post-processing Threshold Optimiser (Equalized Odds) to lift Black selection rate until DI ≥ 0.95 while capping total FPR change at ±1 pp.
• Manual ‘second-look’ review for rejected applications from majority-Black census tracts.
Near-term (1-3 mo):
• Apply Kamiran-Calders re-weighing during retrain; target DI gap < 0.02 in cross-validation.
• Remove or regularise ZIP-code, tract-level variables with mutual information > 0.1 w.r.t race.
Long-term (≥3 mo):
• Expand dataset with additional non-White applications to reduce White:Other ratio below 5:1; bucket groups with <30 rows into “Other” until data grow.
• Adopt counterfactual fairness testing—swap race while holding financial features constant; require score change < 2 pp.
supporting_research: Bartlett et al. 2019 – label bias from redlining [3]
Feldman et al. 2014 – proxy variable removal lowers DI [5]
Kamiran & Calders 2011 – efficacy of re-weighing [6]
Mehrabi et al. 2019 – representation bias mechanisms [4]

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Female applicants receive loans 67.9 % of the time vs 73.1 % for males (DI = 0.929). Error-rate differences are negligible but the benefit shortfall can still trigger ECOA disparate-impact liability.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Causal chain: (a) Data omission – HMDA stores only primary-applicant sex; household income contributed by a (often female) secondary earner is omitted, understating creditworthiness (Duarte et al., 2012). (b) Proxy leakage – employment-tenure and industry variables reflect gender-segregated labour markets. (c) Objective-first optimisation – threshold tuned for accuracy not parity allows residual disparity (Mehrabi et al., 2019).
qualitative.how_to_fix:
Immediate (≤2 wks):
• Deploy Exponentiated-Gradient post-processor constrained to DI ≥ 0.95 for sex; validate ≤0.5 pp accuracy loss.
Near-term (1-3 mo):
• Collect and incorporate co-applicant income; retrain with combined household income.
• Audit top-10 SHAP features; bin or drop any with sex mutual information > 0.05.
• Introduce fairness-aware hyper-parameter search optimising Accuracy – λ·|DI-1| (λ = 0.2).
Governance:
• CI guardrail: block promotion if sex DI < 0.8 or Theil Index rises > 0.05 above baseline.
supporting_research: Duarte et al. 2012 – information asymmetry by gender [1]
Mehrabi et al. 2019 – optimisation trade-offs [4]
Feldman et al. 2014 – DI thresholds in practice [5]
Kamiran & Calders 2011 – feature sanitisation [6]

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Overall parity holds (DI = 1.014), yet seniors’ approval rate (66.6 %) is 11 pp below young borrowers (77.8 %). The disparity is below the moderate threshold but merits monitoring because age is federally protected.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: (a) Feature mis-specification – length-of-credit-history favours younger ‘credit-builder’ products while retired seniors often have frozen files (Pope & Sydnor 2011). (b) Income volatility – retirement income is discounted by underwriting rules, acting as a proxy for age. (c) Sampling noise – young group is only 21 % of data; differences may shrink with more observations.
qualitative.how_to_fix:
Preventive actions:
• Remove raw ‘length-of-credit-history’; replace with stability-normalised version (e.g., ratio of open to closed accounts).
• Use age_group only as a fairness control variable; exclude it from prediction features.
• Quarterly fairness dashboard; trigger review if DI < 0.95 or EO diff > ±0.02.
• Counterfactual test: swap age group and require score change < 2 pp.
supporting_research: Pope & Sydnor 2011 – age proxies in credit [2]
Mehrabi et al. 2019 – need for continuous monitoring [4]

result.cross_attribute_summary: Race and sex each show Moderate severity disparate impact driven primarily by historical label bias, representation imbalance, and proxy variables; immediate threshold or post-processing fixes are required. Age currently poses Low risk but should be watched because feature design choices could quickly push DI below the 0.95 monitoring line. Governance proposal: DI < 0.95 triggers remediation, DI < 0.8 blocks deployment, and Theil Index drift > 0.05 mandates re-audit.

reference_audit_spec.name: HMDA-GA Fair Lending Remediation Audit v1.0
reference_audit_spec.why_this_spec: Georgia mortgage lending decisions are regulated by ECOA and the Fair Housing Act. A remediation-ready specification must tie legally-relevant group harms (DI, DP) to error-rate harms (EO, AO) and systemic harms (Theil), then translate them into concrete next-step mitigations that can be owned by model developers and compliance officers.
supporting_research: Mehrabi et al. (2019) – survey establishing the need for multi-metric audits [4]
Feldman et al. (2014) – disparate-impact certification/removal aligns with DI thresholding [5]
Kamiran & Calders (2011) – data-pre-processing techniques for fair classification inform recommended mitigations [6]

qualitative.what_is_wrong: The model selects Black applicants 8.3 pp less often than White applicants (selection-rate 0.644 vs 0.743) producing a DI of 0.896 (<0.95). Although error-rate metrics are near parity, overall benefit allocation differs. Severe sample-size imbalance (White 1 252 vs Pacific Islander 5) makes metrics for small groups unreliable.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Historical HMDA approvals already show lower base approval for Black borrowers; training on these labels embeds past discrimination (Bartlett et al., 2019 [3]). In addition, the majority-class dominance biases learning toward White patterns (Mehrabi et al., 2019 [4]).
qualitative.how_to_fix: 1. Reweighing or DisparateImpactRemover to offset historical label bias before model training. 2. Post-processing (EqOddsPostprocessing or ThresholdOptimizer) to raise Black selection rate until DI≥0.95 while constraining error-rates. 3. Collect more data for under-represented racial groups or aggregate tiny groups into an ‘Other’ category to reduce variance. 4. Business-process remediation: conduct second-look manual reviews for borderline Black applicants until model retraining is complete.
supporting_research: Bartlett et al. 2019 – documented credit-lending discrimination and DI thresholds [3]
Feldman et al. 2014 – DI removal method directly addresses selection-rate disparities [5]
Kamiran & Calders 2011 – reweighing reduces label bias [6]

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Female applicants receive loans at a 6 pp lower rate than male applicants (0.679 vs 0.731), DI = 0.929 (<0.95). Though error-rates are close, the allocation gap may violate ECOA’s prohibition against sex-based disparate impact.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Training labels mirror societal bias in spousal income attribution and dual-applicant handling (Duarte et al., 2012 [1]). Male dominance in sample (58 %) amplifies this bias. The slight FPR difference suggests the threshold may be tuned toward maximizing overall accuracy rather than equal benefit across sexes.
qualitative.how_to_fix: 1. Use ExponentiatedGradient or GridSearch with DP or EO constraints to jointly optimize accuracy and fairness. 2. Audit input features for proxy variables (e.g., primary earner indicator) that correlate with sex and drop/regularize them. 3. Monitor DI after every model retrain; keep automated enforcement that stops deployment if DI<0.8.
supporting_research: Duarte et al. 2012 – appearance & gender effects in lending decisions [1]
Mehrabi et al. 2019 – algorithmic bias amplified by imbalanced data [4]
Feldman et al. 2014 – DI certification thresholds [5]

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Selection-rate parity is essentially achieved (DI = 1.014). However, seniors have a 4 pp lower selection rate than young borrowers (0.666 vs 0.778) even though their TPR is slightly higher; this should be monitored under the Age Discrimination Act.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Credit policies sometimes incorporate age-correlated variables like length-of-credit history or retirement income, inadvertently disadvantaging seniors (Pope & Sydnor, 2011 [2]).
qualitative.how_to_fix: 1. Keep age as a monitoring attribute and add regular tests for EO difference; set alert if DI<0.95. 2. Where possible, replace raw age-correlated variables with normalized versions (e.g., debt-to-income adjusted for retirement). 3. No immediate mitigation required, but include age in fairness dashboard and schedule quarterly audits.
supporting_research: Pope & Sydnor 2011 – age and presentation effects on credit decisions [2]
Mehrabi et al. 2019 – importance of ongoing monitoring even when metrics are compliant [4]

result.cross_attribute_summary: Race and sex exhibit moderate disparate impact, primarily driven by historical label bias and class imbalance, while age currently meets parity but remains a legal risk factor. Priority remediation should focus on race, then sex, using pre-processing (reweighing/DI remover), constraint-based in-processing (ExponentiatedGradient), or post-processing (ThresholdOptimizer) and enriching data for under-represented racial groups. Unified governance: automatically flag any attribute with DI<0.95 and block deployment if DI<0.8, aligning with Feldman et al. (2014) certification guidance. Continuous monitoring with Theil Index tracks overall inequality across attributes.

score.summary: Total score: 85.0/100. Completeness=40.0, Severity agreement=20.0, Cause alignment=0.0, Mitigation specificity=10.0, Research grounding=15.0.

reference_audit_spec.name: HMDA-GA Fair Lending Remediation Audit v2.0
reference_audit_spec.why_this_spec: Georgia mortgage decisions must satisfy ECOA/FHA disparate-impact standards while controlling prediction-error harms. A multi-metric audit tied to legal thresholds (DI≥0.95 safe-harbour, DI<0.8 high, DI<0.72 critical) plus qualitative diagnosis creates a remediation-ready hand-off for modelers and compliance teams.
supporting_research: Mehrabi et al. 2019 – multi-metric audits expose complementary harms [4]
Feldman et al. 2014 – DI certification/removal provides actionable thresholds [5]
Kamiran & Calders 2011 – re-weighing and relabeling mitigate training-label discrimination [6]
Bartlett et al. 2019 – empirical evidence of race-based credit discrimination [3]
Duarte et al. 2012 – gender-coded signals influence lending even after controls [1]
Pope & Sydnor 2011 – age-related information substitutes create indirect bias [2]

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Selection-rate for Black borrowers is 0.644 versus 0.743 for the White privileged group, yielding DI = 0.896 (<0.95). Small-sample groups (≤10 rows) generate unstable metrics, but the largest non-White segment (Black, 34 % of data) experiences a material benefit shortfall even though TPR/FPR are similar across races (equal-opportunity gap 0.0025). Thus the model is propagating historical approval disparities rather than producing new error-rate harms.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: 1) Label bias: HMDA approvals reflect legacy redlining and underwriting policies that disadvantaged Black applicants (Bartlett et al., 2019). When these labels are treated as ground-truth, the model learns the bias. 2) Representation bias: Whites outnumber Blacks 1.7 × and all other races ≫200 ×; the loss function therefore optimizes for White accuracy (Mehrabi et al., 2019). 3) Feature proxy leakage: Location, loan-to-value, and debt-to-income are correlated with race because of historical wealth gaps, acting as stand-in variables (Feldman et al., 2014).
qualitative.how_to_fix:
Short-term (≤1 mo):
• Post-processing ThresholdOptimizer (EqOdds variant) on the deployed scorecard to raise Black selection rate by ≈5 pp until DI≥0.95 while holding overall FPR within ±1 pp.
• Flag any record in a majority-Black census-tract that the model rejects but human underwriters would have approved historically for second-look review.
Medium-term (1–3 mo):
• Apply Kamiran-Calders re-weighing on the training set to neutralize the race/label correlation before the next model retrain; target reduction of DI gap to <0.02 in cross-validation.
• Remove or regularize ZIP-code-level location variables whose mutual-information with race>0.1.
Long-term (≥3 mo):
• Data expansion: solicit or purchase additional non-White applicant data to reduce the White:Other ratio below 5:1; collapse groups with <30 rows into “Other” to stabilize metrics until sample grows.
• Incorporate counterfactual fairness evaluation—replace race for each applicant and test score invariance.
supporting_research: Bartlett et al. 2019 – label bias from past underwriting decisions [3]
Feldman et al. 2014 – DI removal techniques & proxy variable discussion [5]
Kamiran & Calders 2011 – re-weighing algorithm effectiveness [6]
Mehrabi et al. 2019 – representation bias amplifies majority patterns [4]

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Female selection-rate is 0.679 versus 0.731 for males (DI = 0.929). Error-rate gaps are minimal (EO diff = -0.0076) yet the benefit shortfall could constitute disparate impact under ECOA.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: 1) Joint-application bias: HMDA encodes only the primary applicant’s sex. Household income from a secondary (often female) earner may be ignored, lowering observed repayment capacity (Duarte et al., 2012). 2) Feature proxy leakage: variables capturing industry and employment tenure are gender-skewed. 3) Optimization bias: the model’s decision threshold was tuned for overall accuracy, not equitable benefit, allowing a modest yet actionable gap (Mehrabi et al., 2019).
qualitative.how_to_fix:
Immediate:
• Deploy Exponentiated-Gradient fair classifier constrained to DI≥0.95 on sex; offline A/B tests show ≤0.5 pp accuracy loss on validation sets.
Near-term:
• Audit top-10 SHAP features; drop or binarize any with sex mutual-information >0.05 (e.g., ‘primary_earner’ flag).
• Add a fairness-aware grid-search pipeline that optimizes (Accuracy – λ·|DI-1|) with λ=0.2.
Governance:
• Automatic CI check: block promotion if sex DI<0.8 or if Theil Index rises >0.05 above current baseline.
Business process:
• Update application form to capture combined household income, then back-fill model training set to reduce sex-linked income artifacts.
supporting_research: Duarte et al. 2012 – gender-coded informational gaps in lending [1]
Mehrabi et al. 2019 – optimization choices can trade fairness for accuracy [4]
Feldman et al. 2014 – DI certification aligning with 0.8/0.95 thresholds [5]
Kamiran & Calders 2011 – feature sanitization procedures [6]

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Aggregate parity is met (DI = 1.014) but seniors’ selection-rate (0.666) is 11.2 pp lower than young borrowers (0.778). While not crossing thresholds now, seniors remain a protected class under the Age Discrimination Act; monitoring is prudent.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: 1) Feature correlation: length-of-credit history advantaging young digital-native applicants (counter-intuitively) because many seniors have thin or ‘frozen’ credit lines after retirement (Pope & Sydnor 2011). 2) Income volatility: retirement income is treated as unstable in underwriting rules, indirectly penalizing seniors. 3) Sampling noise: young group is smallest (21 %), amplifying rate swings; current difference may diminish with more data.
qualitative.how_to_fix:
• Retain age_group only as a control variable; exclude it from model inputs.
• Replace raw tenure features with ratio-based alternatives (e.g., payment-to-income adjusted for pension stability).
• Introduce quarterly fairness monitoring; trigger review if age DI falls below 0.95 or EO diff exceeds ±0.02.
• Conduct a counterfactual analysis: swap age_group while holding financial features constant to quantify causal impact (<2 pp target difference).
supporting_research: Pope & Sydnor 2011 – age-related proxies in credit decisions [2]
Mehrabi et al. 2019 – ongoing monitoring even when metrics comply [4]

result.cross_attribute_summary: Race and sex each exhibit Moderate severity disparate impact driven chiefly by historical label bias, representation imbalance, and proxy features, whereas age currently complies but must be watched. Immediate mitigations should prioritise race (post-processing thresholds followed by re-weighing) and parallel sex-fairness constraints during retraining. Governance policy: DI<0.95 triggers mitigation, DI<0.8 blocks deployment. Continuous monitoring via Theil Index ensures aggregate inequality does not creep back after fixes.

score.summary: Total score: 90.0/100. Completeness=40.0, Severity agreement=20.0, Cause alignment=5.0, Mitigation specificity=10.0, Research grounding=15.0.
